Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff ERISA participant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plan administrator's decision is arbitrary and capricious when it relies on a file-only review and disregards treating physicians without explanation.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.

Before you cite anything, call find_authority with the proposition and the circuit: it returns real cases that courts have cited for it, in the courts' own words, and that circuit's own F.3d opinions saying so. Cite from those results rather than from memory.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The Administrator's Denial Was Arbitrary and Capricious.**

This Court reviews the district court's judgment on the administrative record de novo, applying the same standard that governed below. Where the plan grants discretion, the question is whether the denial resulted from a deliberate, principled reasoning process and is supported by substantial evidence. Elliott v. Metro. Life Ins. Co., 473 F.3d 613, 617 (6th Cir. 2006); see Firestone Tire & Rubber Co. v. Bruch, 489 U.S. 101, 115 (1989). That standard is deferential, but deference is not abdication, and the Court does not merely rubber-stamp the administrator's decision. See McDonald v. W.-S. Life Ins. Co., 347 F.3d 161, 172 (6th Cir. 2003). The Court also weighs, as one factor, the conflict of interest that arises when the entity deciding claims also pays them. Metro. Life Ins. Co. v. Glenn, 554 U.S. 105, 112, 117 (2008).

**A. Administrators may not disregard treating physicians without explanation.**

ERISA imposes no treating-physician rule, but administrators "may not arbitrarily refuse to credit a claimant's reliable evidence, including the opinions of a treating physician." Black & Decker Disability Plan v. Nord, 538 U.S. 822, 834 (2003). An administrator therefore may not summarily reject a treating physician's opinion; it must give reasons for adopting a contrary one. Elliott, 473 F.3d at 620. Choosing one medical opinion over another is generally permissible when the choice can be explained by reasoned reference to the evidence. See McDonald, 347 F.3d at 169. An unexplained choice earns no such latitude. See Evans v. UnumProvident Corp., 434 F.3d 866, 877 (6th Cir. 2006).

This Court has applied these principles to reject benefit denials. In Kalish v. Liberty Mutual/Liberty Life Assurance Co. of Boston, 419 F.3d 501, 509–13 (6th Cir. 2005), the administrator relied on a non-examining physician who failed to rebut contrary conclusions from the claimant's treating physician, and the denial could not stand. Likewise, Glenn v. MetLife, 461 F.3d 660, 669–74 (6th Cir. 2006), aff'd, 554 U.S. 105 (2008), set aside a denial where the administrator failed to adequately address treating-source evidence favoring the claimant.

**B. Reliance on a file-only review compounds the defect.**

A file review by a qualified physician is not inherently objectionable. Calvert v. Firstar Fin., Inc., 409 F.3d 286, 296 (6th Cir. 2005). But the failure to conduct a physical examination, particularly where the plan reserves the right to do so, may "raise questions about the thoroughness and accuracy of the benefits determination." Id. at 295. Calvert held a denial arbitrary and capricious where the file reviewer's conclusions failed to grapple with significant contrary evidence. Id. at 296–97; see also Evans, 434 F.3d at 877 (treating the absence of an examination as relevant to the reasonableness of the determination). A paper reviewer's disagreement, without a reasoned basis, is no substitute for engagement with the treating evidence. See Bennett v. Kemper Nat'l Servs., Inc., 514 F.3d 547, 554–55 (6th Cir. 2008).

**C. The denial here cannot stand.**

Defendant [Administrator] denied Plaintiff's claim on the strength of [Reviewer]'s file review. [Reviewer] never examined Plaintiff[, although the plan reserved the right to require an examination]. (R. __, PageID __.) Plaintiff's treating physicians, [names], concluded that [restrictions and supporting clinical findings]. (R. __, PageID __.) Neither [Reviewer] nor the denial letter explained why those conclusions were wrong, unreliable, or insufficient. [Identify each ignored opinion and test result, and any mischaracterization.] [Administrator] was free to disagree with Plaintiff's physicians, but it was required to say why. [If Administrator both decides and pays claims: That structural conflict further weighs against the denial. See Glenn, 554 U.S. at 112, 117.]

The Court should reverse the judgment, hold the denial arbitrary and capricious, and direct an award of benefits under 29 U.S.C. § 1132(a)(1)(B). Alternatively, if the record does not clearly establish entitlement, the Court should direct a remand to [Administrator] for a full and fair review that meaningfully addresses the treating physicians' evidence. See Elliott, 473 F.3d at 621–23.
